name: Battle of Tours
info: On 10 October 732 a Frankish and Aquitanian army under Charles Martel met an Umayyad army under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi between Tours and Poitiers; the Umayyad commander was killed and his army withdrew.

facts.date: 10 October 732 (a Saturday in October, as the Latin chronicles record it)
facts.place: Somewhere between Tours and Poitiers in northern Aquitaine, western France; most historians place it where the rivers Clain and Vienne join, but the exact location is unclear
facts.sides: Franks and Aquitanians under Charles Martel, Mayor of the Palace of Austrasia, against the Umayyad army of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus; numbers are unknown and modern estimates vary widely (Umayyads 20,000 to 80,000; Franks 15,000 to 30,000 or more)
facts.outcome: Abd al-Rahman was killed and the Umayyad army withdrew south; Charles Martel emerged strengthened and Duke Odo weakened.

t: The battle followed two decades of Umayyad conquest from 711, and Duke Odo of Aquitaine, beaten at Bordeaux, appealed to the Franks for help.
Its details, including the numbers and the exact place, are unclear from the surviving sources, and the casualty figures later chroniclers gave are doubtful.
Historians disagree about its weight: some call it a turning point for Europe, others a raid in force that has been turned into a myth.
dyk: The huge Umayyad losses of up to 375,000 that later writers gave for Tours are the same figures the Liber Pontificalis recorded for Odo's victory at Toulouse in 721.
ev: The Umayyads invade the Visigothic Kingdom of the Iberian Peninsula
Duke Odo of Aquitaine breaks the siege of Toulouse and Al-Samh ibn Malik is mortally wounded
Odo allies with the Berber commander Uthman ibn Naissa, who revolts against his Arab masters the next year
Abd al-Rahman defeats Odo at Bordeaux and the Garonne and plunders Bordeaux
Odo appeals to Charles Martel, who agrees to help once Odo accepts Frankish authority
On 10 October, after about a week of skirmishing, the Franks withstand the Umayyad cavalry and Abd al-Rahman is killed
Uqba ibn al-Hajjaj invades Gaul and captures Arles and Avignon
Pepin the Short forces the surrender of Narbonne, ending Umayyad control of Septimania

sections.background:
The Battle of Tours followed two decades of Umayyad conquests in Europe that began in 711 with the invasion of the Visigothic Kingdom of the Iberian Peninsula and were followed by expeditions into the Frankish territories of Gaul. The Umayyads overran Septimania by 719, and Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani made Narbonne his capital from 720. Duke Odo the Great of Aquitaine broke the siege of Toulouse in 721 by surprising the Umayyad forces, and Al-Samh was mortally wounded, but raiding continued, reaching Burgundy in 725. In 730 Odo allied with the Berber commander Uthman ibn Naissa, called Munuza by the Franks, and gave him his daughter Lampagie in marriage. The next year Uthman killed the bishop of Urgell and broke with his Arab masters, and Abd al-Rahman sent an expedition to crush the revolt before turning on Odo.

Odo gathered his army at Bordeaux but was defeated, and Bordeaux was plundered. The Chronicle of 754 said that at the fight on the Garonne “God alone knows the number of the slain”. Odo's troops, like other European troops of the time, had no stirrups and no heavy cavalry, and the Umayyad heavy cavalry broke his infantry in its first charge. Odo then appealed to the Frankish leader, Charles Martel, who granted help only after Odo agreed to submit to Frankish authority. One possible motive for the Umayyad advance north, according to the second continuator of Fredegar's chronicle, was the wealth of the Abbey of Saint Martin of Tours.
sections.forces:
The Umayyad Caliphate was, at the time, perhaps the foremost military power in the world, and Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was its governor of al-Andalus. His army had outpaced its supply wagons and split into raiding parties while the main body advanced more slowly. Charles Martel's Frankish realm was the foremost military power of western Europe. His Austrasian army consisted almost entirely of Rhineland Franks with large auxiliary forces from east of the Rhine, among them Thuringians, Alemanni and Bavarians. He also sent word to the Neustrians and Burgundians, though many Burgundian nobles did not take part, and Frisians were mustered too. The Franks apparently fought without heavy cavalry, and a core of seasoned infantry had fought under Charles for years.

The number of troops on each side is not known. The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754 says the Austrasians were greater in number, but virtually all Western sources estimate the Franks at 30,000, less than half the Muslim force. Edward Creasy, from later Muslim sources, gives the Umayyads as 80,000 or more. Paul K. Davis puts the Umayyads at 80,000 and the Franks at about 30,000, while noting that modern estimates run from 20,000 to 80,000. Edward J. Schoenfeld calls estimates of over fifty thousand Umayyad troops logistically impossible, and Victor Davis Hanson believes both armies were roughly equal at between 20,000 and 30,000. Gore places the Franks at 15,000 to 20,000 and the Muslims at 20,000 to 25,000.
sections.course:
Charles marched south avoiding the old Roman roads, hoping to surprise the Umayyads, and by all accounts they were caught off guard to find a large force in their path to Tours. He chose not to attack but to draw up a defensive formation on high ground, described as phalanx-like; according to Arab sources the Franks formed a large square, with hills and trees in front to break up cavalry charges. For about a week the armies skirmished while the Umayyads waited for their full strength to arrive. The battle began on the seventh day, because Abd al-Rahman, with winter approaching, did not want to wait longer.

Abd al-Rahman trusted in his cavalry and had it charge repeatedly through the day. The Frankish infantry withstood the charges, though according to Arab sources the cavalry broke into the Frankish square several times without breaking it. The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754 says the northern peoples “remained as immobile as a wall” and that the Austrasians killed the king, Abd al-Rahman, striking him on the chest. Night fell and the Franks sheathed their swords until morning. At dawn they found the Arab tents still standing but empty, because the Umayyad army had left silently in the night. Charles Oman wrote that there was no pursuit, as Charles would not let his men leave the line.
sections.aftermath:
Abd al-Rahman was killed and the Umayyad army retreated south over the Pyrenees. Losses are unknown. Later chroniclers claimed that Charles Martel's force lost about 1,500 and that the Umayyads suffered up to 375,000 dead, but the same figures were recorded in the Liber Pontificalis for Odo's victory at Toulouse in 721, and later writers, probably influenced by the Continuations of Fredegar, attributed them to Charles alone. The Vita Pardulfi reports that Abd al-Rahman's forces burned and looted their way through the Limousin on their way home, which suggests that they were not destroyed as the Continuations imply.

Charles went on to extend his power in the south. After Odo's death, about 735, the Aquitanian nobility proclaimed Hunald duke, and Charles confirmed his duchy once Hunald acknowledged him as overlord. In 735 Uqba ibn al-Hajjaj, the new governor of al-Andalus, invaded Gaul, captured Arles and Avignon, and held part of Provence and Septimania for four years. Charles invaded Septimania in 736 and 739 and destroyed an army that tried to relieve Narbonne at the River Berre, but failed to take Narbonne in 737. The Umayyads held parts of Septimania for another 27 years, until Charles's son Pepin the Short forced Narbonne's surrender in 759.
sections.sources:
The surviving sources say little. Few Arab authors refer to the battle, and allusions simply say that Abd al-Rahman and his companions found martyrdom; the Moroccan writer Ibn Idhari, in the 13th century, called the place the path of the martyrs, though Henry Coppée pointed out that the same name was given to the Battle of Toulouse and to other fields where Muslims were defeated. The Latin sources of the 8th and 9th centuries are more numerous but imprecise: most chronicles report the event briefly, saying that Charles fought the Saracens on a Saturday in October. The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, a contemporary Latin source, describes it in greater detail than any other Latin or Arabic source.

The Continuations of Fredegar were composed by Charles Martel's family, and the Latin word they use for their warrior comes from the Book of Maccabees. A passage of Bede may also refer to the battle. The numbers of combatants and the exact location are unclear, and the battlefield lies somewhere between Poitiers and Tours. Ninth-century chroniclers treated the outcome as a divine judgment in Charles's favour and gave him the nickname Martel, the hammer, without tying it to one battle. The casualty figures later given for Tours are those recorded for Toulouse, and modern estimates of army size rest on what the countryside could support, which may be more accurate than the medieval figures.
sections.legacy:
Historians fall broadly into two camps. One, beginning with the Mozarabic Chronicle and the Continuations of Fredegar and carried on by Edward Gibbon, treats Tours as a turning point. Gibbon wrote that the Umayyad advance, had it continued, might have carried the Saracens to the mouth of the Thames, and Hallam, Ranke, Delbrück and Kurth also gave it world importance. William E. Watson holds that it had macrohistorical significance but analyses it militarily, culturally and politically rather than as a simple Muslim against Christian confrontation. It laid foundations of the Carolingian Empire, and Paul Davis says the victory ensured that the Franks would dominate Gaul for more than a century.

The other camp holds that the battle has been overstated. Alessandro Barbero says historians now play down its importance, since the Muslim force aimed to pillage the monastery of Saint-Martin, not to conquer the Frankish kingdom. Tomaž Mastnak calls the saving of Christian Europe a myth built by modern historians, noting that the Fredegar continuators saw one episode among many in Frankish wars for booty and territory. Philip Hitti writes that nothing was decided at Tours, because the Muslim wave had reached a natural limit, and Cowley and Parker say it has been downgraded to a raid in force. Bernard Lewis and Gustave von Grünebaum say Arab historians treat it as minor, while Khalid Blankinship counts it among the defeats that led to the Umayyad caliphate's decline.

summary: At Tours in October 732 a Frankish and Aquitanian army under Charles Martel withstood the cavalry of the Umayyad governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who was killed. Historians still disagree whether it was a turning point for Europe or a raid in force whose importance has been overstated.
notes: Numbers: the article contradicts itself on the Frankish force. The Mozarabic Chronicle is said to give the Austrasians as greater in number, while 'virtually all Western sources' give 30,000, under half the Muslim force. I gave both in the forces section. I also used 'Gore' as the article names him only by surname.

In the facts I wrote 'from 20,000 to 80,000 for the Umayyads' (Davis's summary of modern estimates, the range shared by Hanson 20,000 to 30,000 and Gore 20,000 to 25,000) and '15,000 to 30,000 or more' for the Franks: this is my condensation of Gore (15,000 to 20,000), Davis (about 30,000) and Creasy-type figures. The article also says other estimates run from 30,000 to 80,000 for the Franks. The editor may prefer a plainer line.

The sources section says the casualty figures are those recorded for Toulouse: the article shows only that the same figures are recorded for Toulouse and that later writers attached them to Tours; I have kept to what the article shows. 'May be more accurate than the medieval figures' is the article's own judgement on modern analysis.
Date: the article gives 10 October 732 and says the Latin chronicles give a Saturday in October; it does not say which weekday 10 October 732 was.

Left out: Hitler's table talk section and Speer, D. H. Lawrence's and H. G. Wells's passages, Thalheimer, Haaren, Hugh Kennedy's ghanima remark except significance, the stirrup and feudalism claim of White, the loan from the Pope, the clothing claim, the Byzantine and Bulgarian siege of Constantinople discussion.

In the course section I attribute the 'seventh day' to the article's narrative; Gibbon's version has six days of desultory combat and the Thalheimer version has the fighting renewed the next morning. The Mozarabic Chronicle itself has the fighting in one day and a withdrawal in the night.

The aftermath's 'Odo's death about 735': the article says (c. 735). Hunald's recognition is as the article says, though its account of the sequence is confused (Umayyads entering Provence 'the next year').
